breakthroughs.org: OpenAI model; evaluated by Epoch AI and Thomas Bloom
breakthroughs.summary: Erdős and Turán showed in 1934 that the numbers a+b (a ≠ b in an n-element set) have ≫ log n distinct prime factors, and Erdős asked for anything better. The model proved ≫ n^(1/2) and gave three distinct elementary proofs (exponents 1/8, 1/3 and 1/2), all Lean-checked.

breakthroughs.title: GPT-6 Astra proves the Erdős–Sós conjecture on trees in dense graphs (#548)
breakthroughs.system: GPT-6 Astra (pre-release) in Epoch's FrontierMath Erdős harness
breakthroughs.org: OpenAI model; evaluated by Epoch AI and Thomas Bloom
breakthroughs.summary: The 1962 conjecture says every graph with more than (k−2)n/2 edges contains every tree on k vertices; it was known only in special cases and was called one of the most tantalising problems in extremal graph theory. The model's proof is short and elementary, a double count over vertex orderings with an induction on the tree, and it is Lean-checked. The formal statement differs from the classical one by one edge when (k−1)n is odd. Found with a larger budget than the benchmark's $300 limit.

breakthroughs.title: GPT-6 Astra proves the Erdős–Simonovits rational exponents conjecture (#571)
breakthroughs.system: GPT-6 Astra (pre-release) in Epoch's FrontierMath Erdős harness
breakthroughs.org: OpenAI model; evaluated by Epoch AI and Thomas Bloom
breakthroughs.summary: Shows that for every rational α in [1,2) there is a single bipartite graph G with ex(n;G) ≍ n^α, where earlier work covered only special families of exponents or finite families of graphs (Bukh–Conlon). Bloom calls it the hardest of the model's five FrontierMath Erdős solutions and says he has not yet checked it in detail; confidence rests on the Lean proof. Found with a larger budget than the benchmark's $300 limit.

breakthroughs.title: Disputed claim that Catalan's constant is irrational, with AI-produced numerics and checking
breakthroughs.org: OpenAI models (used by Zhi-Wei Sun, Nanjing University)
breakthroughs.summary: Sun claims a proof adapting the Calegari–Dimitrov–Tang method, with AI producing the numerics and 'verifying' the argument. Wachs (arXiv 2609.22339) computes that a quantity the argument needs to be negative is positive, so the proof is incomplete as written. Graded as if valid; an example of AI checking that did not catch an error.

breakthroughs.title: GPT-6 Astra disproves the 1930 Köthe conjecture in ring theory
breakthroughs.system: GPT-6 Astra (pre-release) in an Epoch AI run over Formal Conjectures' open problems
breakthroughs.org: OpenAI model; run by Tom Adamczewski (Epoch AI)
breakthroughs.summary: In one unsteered attempt (about 26 hours, $432) the model proved in Lean that Krempa's matrix form of the conjecture is false: an algebra over the algebraic closure of F₂ with a nil ideal I and a 2×2 matrix over I that is not nilpotent. A human paper by Adamczewski with ring theorists Böhmler and Marczinzik, who checked the mathematics, then refuted Köthe's original question directly (two nil left ideals whose sum is not nil) and answered a 1989 question of Rowen. Greenfeld, King and Vendramin found another counterexample with some help from the model. Not yet refereed.

breakthroughs.title: GPT-6 Astra disproves Smale's mean value conjecture with constant 1
breakthroughs.system: GPT-6 Astra (pre-release) in an Epoch AI run over Formal Conjectures' open problems
breakthroughs.org: OpenAI model; run by Tom Adamczewski (Epoch AI)
breakthroughs.summary: Smale proved in 1981 that every complex polynomial has a critical point c with |p(z) − p(c)|/|z − c| ≤ 4|p'(z)| and conjectured the constant could be 1. The model gave a Lean-checked polynomial with p(0) = 0, p'(0) = 1 and |p(c)/c| > 1 at every critical point, so the conjecture with K = 1 (and the sharper (d−1)/d form) is false. It took one unsteered attempt of about 15 hours, and Comparator checked the statement against DeepMind's Formal Conjectures file. The witness has very large, unspecified degree and misses by a small margin, so the best constant between 1 and 4 is still open; no complex analyst is on record as having read the proof.

breakthroughs.title: Claude agents produce the first complete Lean proof of Fermat's Last Theorem
breakthroughs.system: Internal Anthropic research model (roughly Claude Fable 5.1 level)
breakthroughs.summary: In 11 days and about six billion output tokens, the model produced a 13-million-line Lean proof of FLT that uses only Lean's three standard axioms, adapting parts of Kevin Buzzard's Imperial FLT project and the flt-regular project. Humans gave only occasional high-level direction. Buzzard called it an extraordinary autoformalisation achievement; it formalises a known theorem and adds no new mathematics.

breakthroughs.title: Bollobás–Nikiforov spectral conjecture proved with GPT-6 Astra; Lean proof by Grok 4.6
breakthroughs.system: GPT-6 Astra (ideation, manuscript) + Grok 4.6 (Lean) + Claude Fable 5.1 (packaging)
breakthroughs.org: OpenAI + xAI (used by Coutinho, Liu, Spier, Tang, Zhang)
breakthroughs.summary: Every noncomplete graph satisfies λ1² + λ2² ≤ 2(1 − 1/ω)m, via a stronger weighted spectral inequality. Ideas from mathematician–Astra exchanges; Grok 4.6 completed the Lean; Palomar registry machine-checked against a Mathlib-only statement. No paper or referee report yet.

breakthroughs.title: AI-assisted, Lean-formalised finite-time blow-up with forcing for Boussinesq and 3D Euler
breakthroughs.system: Claude and OpenAI (Codex) models, unspecified; Lean formalisation
breakthroughs.org: Alpöge and Buckmaster (building on Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa)
breakthroughs.summary: Showed that smooth data with smooth forcing blows up in finite time for the IPM, 2D Boussinesq and 3D incompressible Euler equations, with Lean formalisations. The results were obtained on 15 August and Lean-checked by 22 August using LLMs from both Anthropic and OpenAI, then made public hours before OpenAI's Navier–Stokes claim. Tao calls it a breakthrough that makes forced Navier–Stokes blow-up look feasible. The arguments are heavily AI-assisted and the human-written papers are still being prepared.
breakthroughs.problem: Finite-time blow-up with smooth forcing (IPM, Boussinesq, 3D Euler)

breakthroughs.title: Neural-network search finds a stable self-similar blow-up candidate for unforced 3D Euler
breakthroughs.system: Physics-informed neural networks + spline / interval-arithmetic certification
breakthroughs.summary: PINNs produced a high-precision self-similar singular profile for the unforced Euler equations on ℝ³ with no boundary, which the team is turning into a computer-assisted proof. Their follow-up (arXiv 2609.10860) gives only a preliminary, conditional stability framework, so blow-up is not yet proved. LLMs were used to simplify bounds; Tao hosted the announcement as a guest post.
breakthroughs.problem: Finite-time blow-up for 3D incompressible Euler on ℝ³

breakthroughs.title: OpenAI claims finite-time blow-up for forced 3D Navier–Stokes (Millennium Problem)
breakthroughs.system: Unnamed internal OpenAI model (~10,000 agents) + GPT-6 Astra for the Lean formalisation
breakthroughs.summary: A 166-page paper claims that a 3D Navier–Stokes flow starting at rest, with a smooth force and bounded energy, blows up in finite time (Fefferman's alternatives C and D), with a Lean formalisation. The model is unnamed: OpenAI says only that it is an internal model 'significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra', trained since 28 August through 'large-scale reinforcement learning on top of a previously pretrained model'. About 10,000 agents worked 88 hours (1–5 September) and GPT-6 Astra did the Lean work in 17 hours. The 'Bel' codename comes from an unconfirmed late-August leak about a 10T+ parameter pretrain succeeding 'Doug' (reportedly Astra's base); OpenAI has never named the base, so equating this model with Bel is speculation. Disputed: the unforced problem stays open, Alpöge and Buckmaster posted forced-Euler results hours earlier and raised credit and data-use complaints, and Clay said on 11 September that the problem has 'apparently been settled' without accepting a solution. On 21 September OpenAI said the same model had resolved 100+ other open problems, with no list published.
breakthroughs.model: Unnamed internal OpenAI model (rumoured 'Bel' base, unconfirmed)
breakthroughs.problem: Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness (Clay alternatives C and D)

breakthroughs.title: OpenAI internal model claims finite-time blow-up for unforced 3D Euler from smooth data
breakthroughs.system: Unnamed internal OpenAI model (~100 agents) + GPT-6 Astra for the Lean formalisation
breakthroughs.summary: A companion paper to the Navier–Stokes claim exhibits smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free initial data on ℝ³ whose unforced Euler solution blows up in finite time. That is the open case left by Elgindi's C^(1,α) blow-up and Chen–Hou's result in a bounded cylinder. OpenAI says about 100 agents produced it in roughly 50 hours as a warm-up; it builds on the Córdoba–Martínez-Zoroa amplification method and ships with a Lean certificate in OpenAI's public repository. No refereed or independent written review exists yet, and it drew far less attention than the Navier–Stokes claim.
breakthroughs.problem: Finite-time blow-up for 3D incompressible Euler from smooth data on ℝ³

breakthroughs.title: Rentosertib doses first patient in Phase III, the first for an AI-discovered drug
breakthroughs.summary: GENESIS-IPF-3 is a 52-week, 320-patient, placebo-controlled Phase III at 47 centres in China. It was announced on 2026-07-07 and dosed its first patient on 2026-09-09. The drug and its target were both AI-discovered. 'World's first' is Insilico's own framing, and no Phase III results exist yet.

breakthroughs.title: GPT-5.6 Sol builds a 3-generator 9-relator group with unsolvable word problem
breakthroughs.system: GPT-5.6 Sol Pro (construction); GPT-5.6 Sol in Codex (Lean)
breakthroughs.org: OpenAI (used by Marc Kegel, Shana Yunsheng Li, Qiuyu Ren)
breakthroughs.summary: Beats Borisov's 1969 record (12 relators) with a 3-generator 9-relator presentation with unsolvable word problem; ~28k lines of Lean for the algebraic results.

breakthroughs.title: Core always exists in approval-based committee elections (with GPT-6 Astra)
breakthroughs.summary: Settles the main open question in approval-based multiwinner voting: a core committee always exists and can be found in polynomial time. The authors credit Astra with the primary idea and proof, from a long interactive session. Epoch rates it a 'major advance', but its verifier does not apply (the benchmark asked for an election with an empty core, the opposite of what was proved), so so far only the authors have checked it.
breakthroughs.problem: Core existence in approval-based committee elections

breakthroughs.title: GPT-6 Pro proof of Nivat's 1997 periodicity conjecture, machine-checked in Lean
breakthroughs.system: GPT-6 Pro (proof) + GPT-6 Astra Ultra in Codex (Lean)
breakthroughs.summary: Lean 4/mathlib proof that a 2D configuration with at most mn distinct m×n patterns has a nonzero period; Palomar registry machine-checked it against a Mathlib-only statement. Submitter says GPT-6 Pro found the proof and he is not qualified to digest it. No human expert review yet.

breakthroughs.title: Claude agents flag a CRISPR-like array-associated reverse-transcriptase system (ART)
breakthroughs.summary: From a single high-level prompt, about 950 agents screened 200k+ reverse transcriptases and spotted an unnoticed repeat array beside an RT in a jumbo phage. The resulting array-associated RT system shares traits of programmable DNA-editing systems, but its activity and function are not yet shown. Humans chose which of the agents' reports to pursue and ran the lab work. Preprint.

capex.definition: capex = "Purchases of property and equipment" from the cash-flow statement (cash paid in the quarter; excludes assets acquired under finance leases, operating leases, and PP&E received but not yet paid for). Microsoft: "Additions to property and equipment" (cash). Alphabet: "Purchases of property and equipment". Amazon: gross "Purchases of property and equipment"; Amazon's own "cash capex" quoted on calls is NET of "Proceeds from property and equipment sales and incentives" (about $0.8-1.1B/quarter lower in the 2025-26 quarters shown in the Q2 2026 release). Meta: "Purchases of property and equipment, net" (net of proceeds relating to property and equipment, Meta's presentation since 2024 and in every earnings-release FCF table; 2022-2023 10-Qs showed gross purchases, $0.02-0.13B/quarter higher, recorded in each note). Oracle: "Capital expenditures" (cash); Oracle also reports a lower non-GAAP "net cash outlay for capital expenditures" that subtracts vendor financing and customer prepayments. headline: Microsoft = "capital expenditures including finance leases" from the CFO's remarks (cash PP&E + new finance leases + change in PP&E accrued but not yet paid). Meta = "capital expenditures, including principal payments on finance leases" from each earnings release (= capex + financeLeases here, to within rounding). Alphabet's and Oracle's headline capex equals the cash figure, so no headline field.

financeLeasesBasis.microsoft: New finance leases (ROU assets obtained in exchange for finance-lease liabilities, 10-Q/10-K) through 2025-Q1. From 2025-Q2 (FY25 Q4), when Microsoft began stating the split, the CFO-stated "finance leases" figure is used; it matched the filing figure in FY25 Q4 (6.5 vs 6.503) but ran higher afterwards (the filing figure is in each note). From FY27 (Jul 2026) Microsoft extended datacenter useful lives from 15 to 25 years, which moves some future datacenter leases from finance to operating leases and so out of its headline capex.
financeLeasesBasis.meta: Principal payments on finance leases (financing cash flow). This is NOT the value of new finance leases, but it is exactly what Meta adds to cash capex in its headline figure. Meta stopped tagging new finance-lease ROU assets after 2023.
financeLeasesBasis.amazon: "Property and equipment acquired under finance leases, net of remeasurements and modifications" (supplemental cash-flow disclosure). Amazon's principal repayments of finance leases were much larger in 2022 ($1.5-2.8B/quarter) and are not included.
financeLeasesBasis.google: ROU assets obtained in exchange for finance-lease liabilities; tagged from 2024 only (Alphabet described finance leases as not material for 2022-2023), so earlier quarters are null.

capex.fiscalMapping: Alphabet, Amazon and Meta use calendar fiscal years (quarter = calendar quarter). Microsoft's fiscal year ends June 30, so FY Q1 = Jul-Sep = CY Q3 of the prior calendar year, FY Q2 = Oct-Dec = CY Q4, FY Q3 = Jan-Mar = CY Q1, FY Q4 = Apr-Jun = CY Q2 (e.g. FY26 Q4 = 2026-Q2); these align exactly. Oracle's fiscal year ends May 31. Each Oracle quarter is assigned to the calendar quarter that holds most of it (its midpoint), the same rule Epoch uses: FY Q1 Jun-Aug -> CY Q3, FY Q2 Sep-Nov -> CY Q4, FY Q3 Dec-Feb -> CY Q1 (of the year the quarter ends), and FY Q4 Mar-May -> CY Q2 (e.g. FY27 Q1, Jun-Aug 2026 = 2026-Q3). So Oracle quarters are offset by one month from true calendar quarters.

topToBottomCurve.note: The "line that goes opposite-exponential from top to bottom" best matches Figure 1 of de Grey's 2004 PLoS Biology paper that introduced the phrase "escape velocity". It plots remaining life expectancy against time. People who are 80 or 100 when first-generation rejuvenation therapies arrive follow curves that start flat at the top and plunge ever faster to zero, like a body walking off a cliff. Younger people (50, 30, 0) dip and then curve back up, and that upturn is LEV. The figure is conceptual, with no data behind it. The same shape (flat top, accelerating fall) is also the classic survival curve, which is the best data-backed chart; its data is in dataFile. Candidate 5 is the well-known Wikipedia LEV image. It is a rising exponential (bottom to top), listed in case the memory is mirrored.

candidates.name: "Physical and Actuarial Escape Velocities" (de Grey 2004, PLoS Biology, Fig. 1)
candidates.shape: y = remaining life expectancy, x = time. Curves for ages 100 and 80 fall from top to bottom ever faster; curves for 50, 30 and 0 bottom out and then rise (escape velocity).
candidates.whyItFits: It is the original LEV chart, and its falling curves are exactly "top to bottom, opposite-exponential".
candidates.source: de Grey ADNJ (2004), "Escape velocity: why the prospect of extreme human life extension matters now", PLoS Biol 2(6):e187. CC BY 4.0.
candidates.data: No data behind it. A real-data version: follow one cohort along the diagonal of period life tables, plotting remaining life expectancy e(age0 + k, year0 + k) against year0 + k. A flat or rising segment would be LEV. See derived.cohortRemainingLE.

candidates.name: Survival curves by era (share of a birth cohort alive at each age), "rectangularization"
candidates.shape: Starts at 100% at age 0 and stays high, then falls steeply after ~70. Gompertz mortality makes the late drop look like an exponential flipped top to bottom. Across eras the curve becomes more rectangular.
candidates.whyItFits: It has the same top-to-bottom accelerating fall and is often shown in LEV and longevity talks. It is fully data-backed.
candidates.source: Human Mortality Database period life tables (l(x), radix 100,000), England and Wales, via Our World in Data's catalog.
candidates.data: dataFile (England and Wales 1851, 1900, 1950, 2000, 2022; ages 0, 1, 5, 10 ... 110; survivingPct = l(x)/1000). The quantile form covers 46 countries, 1751-2024: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/survival-ages-across-the-population.csv (plot x = age value, y = percentile).

candidates.name: Remaining life expectancy vs age
candidates.shape: Declines from e0 (~81-85) toward ~2 years at 100. LEV would appear as this curve lifting year after year by at least as much as people age.
candidates.whyItFits: It is a top-to-bottom curve and is the quantity LEV is defined on, but its shape is convex rather than a cliff.
candidates.data: https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/remaining-life-expectancy-at-different-ages.csv (ages 0/10/15/25/45/65/80); all ages 0-110 are in dataUrl (life_expectancy column).

candidates.name: Gompertz mortality-rate curve shown inverted
candidates.shape: Death probability rises roughly exponentially with age (doubling every ~8 years). Flipped, it becomes a top-to-bottom exponential.
candidates.whyItFits: It is literally an "opposite exponential", but it is rarely drawn inverted.
candidates.source: HMD q(x) in dataUrl (probability_of_death, in %). The WHO GHO 5-year age groups are also available.

candidates.name: Wikipedia "Longevity Escape Velocity" image (User:Zedatik, 2012, public domain)
candidates.shape: A rising exponential, with "life expectancy gained via advancing technologies" against "advancing technologies", crossing a dashed "Longevity escape velocity" line. It goes bottom to top, not top to bottom.
candidates.whyItFits: It is the most-viewed LEV image, so it is worth ruling in or out with the user.

cohortRemainingLE.method: Japan, both sexes, HMD period life tables from dataUrl. For a person aged A in 1973, the table gives remaining life expectancy e(A+k) in year 1973+k, for k = 0, 5, 10, ... "noProgress" reads the same ages off the fixed 1973 table, i.e. what would happen with no medical progress since 1973. Actual minus noProgress is the progress already banked. LEV requires the actual curve to stop falling.

levGauge.method: OLS slope of period remaining life expectancy at 65 (e65) over the last 21 HMD years. LEV at 65 would need a slope of 1.0 or more years per year.
levGauge.note: HMD and OWID's combined HMD+UN WPP series can differ slightly (Japan e65 2023: HMD 22.08, OWID CSV 22.49). Pick one source per chart.

recordTrend.note: This is the Oeppen-Vaupel "broken limits" line: about 3 months of record life expectancy gained per calendar year for 180 years, slowing since 1950. LEV needs at least 1.0 year per year in REMAINING life expectancy, roughly 4x the historic record pace at birth and 10-20x the recent pace at age 65 (0.04-0.10 years/year; see topToBottomCurve.derived.levGauge).
